headline: The AI Memory System That Scored 100% — With Caveats
lede: Developer Ben Sigman and actress Milla Jovovich launched MemPalace, an open-source AI memory layer that stores AI conversations verbatim and organizes them into a navigable “palace” of wings, halls, and rooms. The launch claimed perfect scores on three industry benchmarks and a novel lossless compression technique. Swift technical scrutiny dismantled most of those claims — several of which Sigman publicly corrected within twenty-four hours.
body:
MemPalace is a Python memory layer for AI assistants built around a philosophically coherent idea: instead of using an AI to decide what a conversation was worth remembering — discarding reasoning alongside noise — store every exchange verbatim in *ChromaDB*, a local *vector database*, and retrieve relevant passages at query time via *semantic search*. The system organizes stored memories into a hierarchy of wings, halls, and rooms, inspired by the ancient *method of loci* mnemonic technique. The local-first design is genuine: no API keys, no cloud sync, a single installable dependency, MIT licensed.

**The 100% LongMemEval score** warrants the most scrutiny. *LongMemEval* is a legitimate peer-reviewed benchmark (ICLR 2025) testing five long-term memory abilities across 500 questions embedded in multi-session chat histories. MemPalace identified the seventeen questions it was failing, engineered targeted patches for each specific case, and retested on the same dataset — a process the project’s own documentation later called “the benchmark equivalent of teaching to the test.” The honest held-out result on a separate set is 98.4%. More fundamentally, the 96.6% “raw” score anchoring comparisons to Mem0 and Zep measures ChromaDB’s default embedding model on uncompressed text, with the palace architecture entirely inactive. When palace features are enabled, recall drops to 89.4%. An independent replication using plain ChromaDB with no MemPalace code whatsoever reproduced 93.8% — suggesting the palace metaphor, whatever its user-experience appeal, does not improve retrieval.

The third perfect score, on *LoCoMo* (a long-conversation benchmark from **Snap** (SNAP) Research, ACL 2024), is the most straightforwardly misleading. MemPalace was run with a retrieval window of 50 on a dataset containing only 19–32 items per conversation, making 100% mathematically guaranteed — every candidate was returned by default. The realistic score with standard parameters is 60.3% *recall@10*. The *ConvoMem* result — cited as “2x Mem0’s score” — was evaluated on 300 items drawn from a 75,336-item dataset, providing no statistical basis for the claimed advantage. The “30x lossless **AAAK** compression” claim also collapsed: AAAK is a custom text-shortening format based on regex entity detection and sentence scoring that is demonstrably lossy — enabling it drops LongMemEval recall by 12.4 percentage points. Sigman corrected the lossless label publicly within a day.

Jovovich’s co-creator credit is genuine but narrow. She conceived the palace metaphor and performed implementation work through Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding assistant, which she used as her primary development tool — something she acknowledged openly in the project’s own forums, noting she had never run a git pull before the project began. Sigman handled the substantive engineering. The community audit that followed drew a pointed conclusion: the palace hierarchy has no measurable effect on retrieval ranking, AAAK mode actively hurts performance, and the LoCoMo result is trivially reproducible by any retrieval system. That Sigman acknowledged the main errors the same day is to his credit; the original marketing language did not prepare users for any of these caveats.

Strip the inflated benchmarks and what remains is a real open-source project with a coherent philosophy. Human memory preserves journeys as well as destinations — the alternatives considered, the reasons for changing course — and AI summarization systems discard precisely that texture. Storing conversations verbatim and indexing them semantically is not MemPalace’s invention, but the project packages the approach cleanly with a minimal local install and an architecture that could, in principle, evolve into something closer to the navigable memory palace its authors envision. The gap between that vision and the current retrieval reality is the work still ahead.

concepts.definition: A peer-reviewed benchmark (ICLR 2025) for AI long-term memory systems. It embeds 500 curated questions inside multi-session chat histories up to 1.5 million tokens long and tests five abilities: information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention. State-of-the-art commercial systems scored 30–70% when the benchmark launched.

A long-conversation memory benchmark from Snap Research (ACL 2024) built from multi-session dialogues of up to 35 conversations and 300 turns. It tests whether a system can retrieve and reason about events mentioned far earlier in a long conversation history. Results depend heavily on the retrieval window parameter (top_k) relative to dataset size.

A large-scale conversational memory benchmark (arXiv 2511.10523) comprising 75,336 question-answer pairs across six memory categories, including user facts, temporal changes, and implicit inference. Results sampled from only a small fraction of the full dataset carry no statistical validity for cross-system comparisons.

A proprietary text-shortening format developed for MemPalace that uses regex entity detection and sentence-importance scoring to produce structured English abbreviations (e.g., ‘PRI(lead) | KAI(backend,3yr)’). Marketed at launch as 30× lossless compression; subsequently acknowledged by the creators to be lossy summarization, with measurable recall degradation.

An ancient mnemonic technique in which the memorizer mentally places items inside familiar architectural spaces — rooms in a house, stops on a known walk. Recall is triggered by mentally navigating the space. MemPalace borrows the metaphor to organize AI memories into wings, halls, rooms, and drawers, though the architectural hierarchy currently has no measurable effect on retrieval performance.

An open-source, locally runnable vector database designed for storing and searching text embeddings. It converts text into numerical vectors and retrieves documents whose vectors are semantically closest to a query vector, enabling meaning-based rather than keyword-based search.

A retrieval method that matches documents to queries by meaning rather than exact keywords. Text is encoded as numerical vectors, and results are ranked by vector similarity — so a query about “dog food” can surface a document mentioning “pet nutrition” without sharing a single word.

A retrieval metric measuring what fraction of relevant documents appear in the top k results returned by a search system. recall@5 asks: is the right answer somewhere in the first five results? It does not measure whether a system can generate a correct answer from those results — a distinction that makes comparisons to end-to-end answer-accuracy scores misleading.

An approach to AI memory that saves the full, unedited text of conversations rather than extracting summaries or key facts. The rationale is that AI summarization discards reasoning and nuance; verbatim storage trades storage efficiency for retrieval completeness, deferring the compression decision to search time.

A database that stores data as dense numerical vectors (embeddings) and retrieves items by geometric proximity rather than exact match. It is the infrastructure underlying most modern AI semantic-search systems. Vector databases trade keyword precision for semantic flexibility.

repos.summary: MemPalace is an open-source Python memory layer for AI assistants. It stores AI conversation transcripts verbatim in ChromaDB, organizes them into a hierarchical palace of wings, halls, and rooms, and retrieves relevant passages via semantic search. The project runs entirely locally with no API keys required, carries a single dependency, and is MIT licensed.

fact_check: Multiple claims in the launch post are false or materially misleading. (1) The 100% LongMemEval score was produced by identifying the seventeen failing test questions, patching them specifically, and retesting on the same set — a form of overfitting the project’s own documentation later acknowledged; the held-out score is 98.4%. (2) The 96.6% raw score measures ChromaDB’s default embeddings on uncompressed text with the palace architecture inactive; enabling palace features drops recall to 89.4%, and plain ChromaDB with no MemPalace code at all reproduced 93.8%. (3) The 100% LoCoMo score is trivially guaranteed: the retrieval window was set larger than the entire candidate pool, returning everything by default. (4) AAAK compression is lossy, not lossless — confirmed by a 12.4 percentage-point recall drop and publicly acknowledged by Sigman within twenty-four hours. (5) The ConvoMem result was generated from 300 items (0.4% of the benchmark), providing no valid statistical basis for comparing with Mem0’s published score.
